title: The Joint Pain Pill Millions Take May Be Accelerating Alzheimer's. A 60,000-Patient Study Just Flagged It.
excerpt: Glucosamine, one of the world's most popular over-the-counter supplements, is linked to a 25 per cent faster progression from mild cognitive impairment to dementia — and the mechanism may involve sugar molecules hijacking brain proteins.
body:
Glucosamine is one of those supplements that lives in almost every medicine cabinet. Parents take it. Grandparents swear by it. Walk into any Indian grocery store in New Jersey or Fremont, and you will find it next to the turmeric and fish oil. For decades, the over-the-counter pill has been the default answer to creaky knees and stiff joints — a harmless daily habit, or so millions assumed.

A study published this week in *Nature Metabolism* suggests that assumption may need urgent re-examination. Researchers at the University of Florida analysed electronic health records from nearly 60,000 patients with varying degrees of cognitive decline and found that regular glucosamine use was associated with a **25 per cent higher likelihood** of progressing from mild cognitive impairment to full-blown dementia.

Among patients who already had an Alzheimer's or dementia diagnosis, glucosamine use was also linked to a **25 per cent increase in the likelihood of death** during the study period — a finding that startled even the researchers who uncovered it.

## The Sugar Molecule Problem

The mechanism the team identified is not speculative. Glucosamine is a sugar-related molecule, and it can cross the blood-brain barrier. Once inside the brain, it appears to exacerbate a damaging process called hyperglycosylation — the abnormal attachment of sugar molecules to proteins that are essential for neurological function.

"Proteins are the cell's molecular machines, and many of them need sugar tags added in just the right way to fold correctly, travel to the right place and do their jobs," said Matt Gentry, chair of biochemistry and molecular biology at the University of Florida. "When that process goes haywire, the consequences for brain health can be severe."

In animal experiments conducted alongside the human data analysis, the researchers confirmed that glucosamine worsened this glycosylation process in brain tissue — adding a biological layer to what the patient records were already showing.

A commentary published alongside the study in *Nature Metabolism* noted that the findings suggest glycosylation pathways could be a **targetable mechanism** for future Alzheimer's treatments — a potential silver lining in an otherwise alarming discovery.

## Not Proof, but a Serious Signal

Gentry was careful to note the limits of the finding. "While it's an association and not proof of causality, it does raise an important clinical question that now deserves much more attention," he said.

The study used AI tools to comb through 12 years of University of Florida health system records, from 2012 to 2024. Roughly 8 per cent of patients with declining brain function were found to be taking glucosamine — a meaningful proportion given how widely the supplement is used.

Notably, among patients with only mild cognitive impairment and no established dementia, the increased mortality risk was not observed, suggesting that glucosamine's most dangerous effects may be concentrated in people whose brains are already under significant stress.

## Why This Matters for South Asian Families

The finding lands with particular force in the Indian diaspora. Joint pain — especially knee osteoarthritis — is disproportionately common among South Asians, driven by genetic predisposition, dietary factors, and lifestyle patterns. Glucosamine and chondroitin supplements are routinely recommended by doctors in India and widely purchased by NRIs for themselves and their ageing parents.

At the same time, South Asians face elevated baseline risks for Alzheimer's and vascular dementia, linked to higher rates of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome — conditions that already put the brain under glycaemic stress.

The combination of high glucosamine usage and high dementia vulnerability makes this population uniquely exposed to the risk the study describes.

The Arthritis Foundation continues to list glucosamine as a supplement that may help with joint inflammation, and no regulatory body has issued a warning or recall. But for families managing both joint pain and cognitive decline in ageing relatives, the study opens a difficult conversation about whether a routine supplement may be doing more harm than good.

Until larger, controlled trials can establish or rule out a causal link, the most prudent step may be the simplest: talk to a doctor before continuing glucosamine — especially if mild cognitive impairment has already been diagnosed.
